prompt: Which of these jobs is done by the processor?
optionA: Keeping files so they survive a restart
optionB: Carrying out the instructions a program contains
optionC: Deciding which program is allowed to run next
optionD: Holding the pictures shown on the screen
correctAnswerText: Carrying out the instructions a program contains
explanation: The processor executes instructions; that is what it is for. Keeping files is storage, deciding what runs next is the operating system's decision, and holding an image is memory.

prompt: Is the processor where a computer's files are kept?
optionA: Yes; the processor holds everything the machine has
optionB: Yes, but only the files currently open
optionC: No; files are kept in the operating system
optionD: No; files are kept on storage, and the processor holds almost nothing
correctAnswerText: No; files are kept on storage, and the processor holds almost nothing
explanation: The processor works on values handed to it and keeps only a few at a time. Confusing it with storage makes the rest of the machine's arrangement impossible to explain.

prompt: Is the processor hardware or software?
optionA: Hardware; it is a physical component
optionB: Software; it is a set of instructions
optionC: Software; it is part of the operating system
optionD: Neither; it is a way of describing what a machine does
correctAnswerText: Hardware; it is a physical component
explanation: The processor is a physical part that instructions are given to. Instructions are what run on it, which is exactly the distinction the question turns on.

prompt: A machine displays an image on screen. Which part of that is the processor's job?
optionA: Holding the image while it is displayed
optionB: Turning the values into light on the panel
optionC: Working out the values that describe the image
optionD: Deciding which application may use the screen
correctAnswerText: Working out the values that describe the image
explanation: The processor computes; other parts hold the result, display it, and arbitrate access to it. Attributing everything the machine does to the processor is the error being probed.

prompt: Which component mainly executes program instructions?
optionA: Working memory
optionB: The processor
optionC: The storage drive
optionD: The keyboard
correctAnswerText: The processor
explanation: Instructions are fetched from memory and carried out by the processor. Memory holds them and storage keeps them between runs; neither performs them.

prompt: Two numbers are added together. Which unit performs the addition?
optionA: The control unit
optionB: Working memory
optionC: The operating system
optionD: The arithmetic and logic unit
correctAnswerText: The arithmetic and logic unit
explanation: The arithmetic and logic unit is the part built to carry arithmetic out. The control unit decides what happens next, memory holds the values, and the operating system issues no arithmetic of its own here.

prompt: Two values are compared to see which is larger. Which unit performs the comparison?
optionA: The arithmetic and logic unit, which handles logic as well as arithmetic
optionB: The control unit, since a comparison controls what happens next
optionC: Working memory, where the two values are held
optionD: The operating system, which decides the outcome
correctAnswerText: The arithmetic and logic unit, which handles logic as well as arithmetic
explanation: The unit's name covers logic as well as arithmetic, and a comparison is a logic operation. That its result then influences what runs next is a separate step performed by the control unit.

prompt: What does the control unit do?
optionA: Performs the calculations the instructions ask for
optionB: Holds the program while it runs
optionC: Works out what each instruction means and directs the other parts accordingly
optionD: Stores the results of each instruction
correctAnswerText: Works out what each instruction means and directs the other parts accordingly
explanation: The control unit interprets and directs; it produces no values of its own. Reading "control" as "does the work" is exactly the misreading the name invites.

prompt: An instruction says to multiply two values. Which part decides that a multiplication is what is wanted, and which part produces the answer?
optionA: The arithmetic and logic unit decides and produces the answer
optionB: The control unit decides; the arithmetic and logic unit produces the answer
optionC: The control unit decides and produces the answer
optionD: Working memory decides; the control unit produces the answer
correctAnswerText: The control unit decides; the arithmetic and logic unit produces the answer
explanation: Interpreting the instruction and performing it are two jobs done by two parts. Assigning both to one of them collapses the distinction the two units exist to make.

prompt: What do registers hold?
optionA: The whole of the program currently running
optionB: Files that must survive a restart
optionC: A copy of everything in working memory
optionD: The few values the processor is working with at this moment
correctAnswerText: The few values the processor is working with at this moment
explanation: Registers hold a very small number of values, right where the work happens. Anything larger lives further out, in memory or on storage.

prompt: How do registers compare with working memory?
optionA: Far faster and far smaller
optionB: Faster and larger
optionC: Slower and smaller
optionD: The same speed, and simply nearer
correctAnswerText: Far faster and far smaller
explanation: Speed and capacity run in opposite directions across the whole arrangement, and registers sit at the fast, tiny end of it. Being both faster and larger would remove the reason for having memory at all.

prompt: What happens to the contents of working memory when a machine is switched off?
optionA: They are kept until the machine is switched on again
optionB: They are written to storage automatically
optionC: They are lost
optionD: They are kept for a few hours and then lost
correctAnswerText: They are lost
explanation: Working memory holds what is needed while the machine runs and keeps nothing without power. That is precisely why saving a file writes it somewhere else.

prompt: Which of these is kept in working memory while a program runs?
optionA: The program's files, permanently
optionB: The values the program is currently using
optionC: The operating system's installation, permanently
optionD: Nothing; a running program uses only the processor
correctAnswerText: The values the program is currently using
explanation: Working memory holds what is in use now, and gives it up when the program ends. Permanent copies of anything live on storage.

prompt: Does adding more working memory make the processor faster?
optionA: Yes; more memory means faster calculation
optionB: Yes; the processor runs at the speed of the memory
optionC: No; adding memory has no effect on anything
optionD: No; it lets more be held at once, which is a different thing
correctAnswerText: No; it lets more be held at once, which is a different thing
explanation: More memory removes the need to shuffle data to and from storage, which can make a machine feel much faster without the processor doing anything more quickly. The two are separate quantities.

prompt: A machine has plenty of storage and very little working memory. What is the likely effect?
optionA: Programs run, but the machine spends much of its time moving data between memory and storage
optionB: Programs cannot be installed at all
optionC: Programs run at full speed, since storage makes up the difference
optionD: The processor runs more slowly to compensate
correctAnswerText: Programs run, but the machine spends much of its time moving data between memory and storage
explanation: Storage can stand in for memory and is far slower, so the work still happens and takes much longer. Installation depends on storage, which the machine has.

prompt: A value must still be available after the machine has been switched off and on again. Where should it be kept?
optionA: In working memory
optionB: In a processor register
optionC: On storage
optionD: In the processor cache
correctAnswerText: On storage
explanation: Only storage keeps its contents without power. Each of the other three is faster and loses everything when the machine stops.

prompt: A value is read millions of times while a program runs and does not need to survive the program ending. Where is it best kept?
optionA: On storage, so that it is safe
optionB: In working memory, or nearer the processor still
optionC: On storage, since it is read so often
optionD: Nowhere; a value read that often should be recomputed each time
correctAnswerText: In working memory, or nearer the processor still
explanation: The requirement is speed and not survival, which points inward rather than outward. Keeping it on storage would make every one of those millions of reads far slower for a guarantee nobody asked for.

prompt: Order these from fastest to slowest: working memory, a processor register, a storage drive.
optionA: Working memory, register, storage drive
optionB: Storage drive, working memory, register
optionC: Register, storage drive, working memory
optionD: Register, working memory, storage drive
correctAnswerText: Register, working memory, storage drive
explanation: Speed increases with nearness to the processor, so registers lead and storage trails. The ordering by capacity runs the other way.

prompt: Order the same three from largest capacity to smallest.
optionA: Storage drive, working memory, register
optionB: Register, working memory, storage drive
optionC: Working memory, storage drive, register
optionD: They are all about the same size
correctAnswerText: Storage drive, working memory, register
explanation: Capacity runs opposite to speed, so the slowest layer is the largest. Getting both orders the same way round is the answer that shows the trade-off has not landed.

prompt: Someone proposes building a machine whose memory is as fast as a register and as large as a storage drive. Every layer of the existing arrangement exists because no such thing is available. What is wrong with the proposal?
optionA: Nothing; such memory already exists and is simply not used
optionB: Registers cannot be made larger under any circumstances
optionC: Nothing is wrong with wanting it; the arrangement exists precisely because speed and capacity cannot both be maximised affordably
optionD: A single layer would be slower than several
correctAnswerText: Nothing is wrong with wanting it; the arrangement exists precisely because speed and capacity cannot both be maximised affordably
explanation: The proposal describes exactly what would make the hierarchy unnecessary, which is why the hierarchy exists. The obstacle is cost and physics rather than an oversight in how machines are built.

prompt: A machine's cache is described as being larger than its working memory. Every other layer in the machine follows the usual arrangement. Why is that description suspect?
optionA: Cache and memory are the same thing under two names
optionB: Cache sits nearer the processor than memory, so it is faster and correspondingly smaller
optionC: Cache is always exactly half the size of memory
optionD: Nothing is suspect; cache size varies freely
correctAnswerText: Cache sits nearer the processor than memory, so it is faster and correspondingly smaller
explanation: Each layer trades capacity for speed against the one beyond it, and cache is on the fast side of memory. A layer that was both faster and larger would make the layer beyond it pointless.

prompt: Which pair contains one input device and one output device?
optionA: Monitor and speaker
optionB: Mouse and scanner
optionC: Printer and speaker
optionD: Keyboard and monitor
correctAnswerText: Keyboard and monitor
explanation: A keyboard brings data in and a monitor sends it out. Each of the other pairs has both devices travelling in the same direction.

prompt: A touchscreen displays images and registers where it is touched. How should it be classified?
optionA: Both input and output
optionB: Output only, because it is a screen
optionC: Input only, because it is touched
optionD: Neither, because it does both
correctAnswerText: Both input and output
explanation: Classification follows what the data does, and here it travels in both directions. Deciding from the device category rather than from the data is what makes a screen look like output only.

prompt: A storage drive has data written to it and read from it. How should it be classified?
optionA: Neither; storage is a separate category
optionB: Output only, since data is written to it
optionC: Both input and output
optionD: Input only, since data is read from it
correctAnswerText: Both input and output
explanation: Data travels into the drive and back out of it, so both directions occur. Treating storage as a category outside the classification is the answer that avoids applying the rule at all.

prompt: What does a bus do?
optionA: Stores data on the way between components
optionB: Carries signals between components along a shared route
optionC: Connects exactly two components to each other
optionD: Converts data from one form to another
correctAnswerText: Carries signals between components along a shared route
explanation: A bus is a route rather than a place, and several components share it. Storing anything is the job of memory, and a shared route is what makes a bus different from a direct connection.

prompt: A value is read from memory into the processor. Besides the value itself, what else must travel?
optionA: Nothing else; the value alone is enough
optionB: The whole of the surrounding memory, from which the value is picked
optionC: The instruction that asked for the value
optionD: Which location is wanted, and a signal saying that a read is what is being asked for
correctAnswerText: Which location is wanted, and a signal saying that a read is what is being asked for
explanation: Memory has to be told where to look and what to do, so an address and a control signal accompany the data. Believing only data travels is the half-formed model this measures.

prompt: Put the stages of handling one instruction in order.
optionA: Fetch, decode, execute
optionB: Decode, fetch, execute
optionC: Fetch, execute, decode
optionD: Execute, fetch, decode
correctAnswerText: Fetch, decode, execute
explanation: An instruction has to be collected before it can be interpreted, and interpreted before it can be carried out. Decoding first would require understanding something not yet obtained.

prompt: How many times does that sequence of stages run while a program of a thousand instructions executes?
optionA: Once, covering the whole program
optionB: Three times, once per stage
optionC: About a thousand times, once for each instruction
optionD: Once per line of source code the programmer wrote
correctAnswerText: About a thousand times, once for each instruction
explanation: The cycle handles a single instruction and repeats for the next, which is what makes a processor able to run a program of any length. Treating it as covering the whole program misses the repetition entirely.

prompt: An instruction adds a value held in memory to one already in the processor. Where does the memory value go first?
optionA: Straight into the arithmetic and logic unit from memory
optionB: Into a register inside the processor
optionC: Onto storage, and then into the processor
optionD: Into the control unit, which performs the addition
correctAnswerText: Into a register inside the processor
explanation: Values are brought into registers before they are operated on, which is what registers are for. The arithmetic unit works on what the registers hold rather than reaching into memory itself.

prompt: A result has just been computed. Someone says it is written directly to the storage drive. The program did not ask for anything to be saved. Where does it actually go?
optionA: To the storage drive, as they said
optionB: Back into the control unit for checking
optionC: Nowhere; it is used and discarded within the arithmetic unit
optionD: Into a register, and then to memory if the program keeps it
correctAnswerText: Into a register, and then to memory if the program keeps it
explanation: Reaching storage requires an explicit request, and none was made. A computed value lands in a register and travels no further unless the program stores it.

prompt: A single instruction is traced and the value appears never to enter a register at all, going straight from memory to the arithmetic unit. Every other instruction in the trace does use a register. What is the likely explanation?
optionA: The trace has omitted the step; the register is where operands are held for the arithmetic unit
optionB: This instruction is a special kind that bypasses registers
optionC: The arithmetic unit contains its own memory for such cases
optionD: The value was small enough not to need a register
correctAnswerText: The trace has omitted the step; the register is where operands are held for the arithmetic unit
explanation: One instruction behaving unlike every other in the same trace points at the record rather than at the machine. Operands reach the arithmetic unit through registers, and the size of a value does not change that.

prompt: Trace where a value is at each point while one instruction adds it to another: it begins on the storage drive and the program has just started. What is the full path?
optionA: Storage to the arithmetic unit, result to memory
optionB: Storage to a register, register to memory, memory to the arithmetic unit
optionC: Storage to memory, memory to a register, register to the arithmetic unit, result back to a register
optionD: Memory to the arithmetic unit, result to storage
correctAnswerText: Storage to memory, memory to a register, register to the arithmetic unit, result back to a register
explanation: Each layer hands on to the next one inward, and the result comes back out the way it went in. Skipping memory or reaching the arithmetic unit from storage removes a step the machine cannot do without.

prompt: A value is used repeatedly by a tight piece of code. Where would you expect it to be after the first few uses, and why?
optionA: Written back to storage after each use, for safety
optionB: In a register or cache, because the machine keeps recently used values near the processor
optionC: In working memory, since that is where all values live
optionD: Recomputed each time, since holding it costs space
correctAnswerText: In a register or cache, because the machine keeps recently used values near the processor
explanation: Repeated use is exactly the condition the inner layers exist for, so a value read again and again is kept close. Writing it out after each use would pay the largest cost available on every use.

prompt: Which digit values are used in binary?
optionA: 0 to 9
optionB: 1 and 2
optionC: A and B
optionD: 0 and 1
correctAnswerText: 0 and 1
explanation: Binary uses exactly two digit values. Everything a machine holds — numbers, text, images, sound — is built from them.

prompt: The same pattern of bits is opened as a number by one program and as text by another, and each shows something different. How is that possible?
optionA: The bits carry no meaning of their own; what they represent is decided by how they are interpreted
optionB: One of the two programs has misread the bits
optionC: The bits change depending on which program opens them
optionD: Text and numbers are stored in different ways, so one of the two is wrong
correctAnswerText: The bits carry no meaning of their own; what they represent is decided by how they are interpreted
explanation: Storage holds patterns and nothing else, and meaning is supplied by whatever reads them. This is why opening a file with the wrong program shows nonsense rather than reporting an error.

prompt: A machine copying large files between drives shows the processor almost idle throughout. Which component limits the work?
optionA: The processor
optionB: Working memory
optionC: The drives
optionD: The display
correctAnswerText: The drives
explanation: An idle processor cannot be what is holding the work up. Copying moves data between drives and is limited by how fast they can read and write it.

prompt: A task takes far longer than expected. The processor sits near idle, the drives are busy continuously, and there is ample free memory. Someone proposes a faster processor. Would it help?
optionA: Yes; a faster processor speeds up every task
optionB: No; the processor is not what the work is waiting on, so a faster one would sit idle just as often
optionC: Yes; the drives would be driven harder by a faster processor
optionD: No; more memory is what is needed
correctAnswerText: No; the processor is not what the work is waiting on, so a faster one would sit idle just as often
explanation: The evidence names the busy component and the idle one, which settles where the limit is. Adding memory would not help either, since the stem says there is already plenty.

prompt: A calculation runs slowly. The processor is fully used, the drives are quiet and memory is largely free. Which change would help most?
optionA: A larger storage drive
optionB: More working memory
optionC: A faster network connection
optionD: A faster processor, or spreading the work across more of them
correctAnswerText: A faster processor, or spreading the work across more of them
explanation: The fully used component is the one holding the work up, and here it is the processor. Each other change addresses a resource the evidence shows is not under pressure.

prompt: A machine is upgraded with a much faster processor and the task it was bought for runs barely faster. What does that tell you, and what should be measured next?
optionA: The processor was not the limit; measure which component is busy while the task runs
optionB: The upgrade was faulty and should be replaced
optionC: The task cannot be made faster by any hardware
optionD: The processor must be faster still
correctAnswerText: The processor was not the limit; measure which component is busy while the task runs
explanation: An upgrade that changes nothing is evidence about where the limit is not, which narrows the search rather than exhausting it. Buying a faster version of the same component again is what the observation argues against.

prompt: After a component is upgraded and the task speeds up, the same task is now limited by a different component. Is that a sign the upgrade was wrong?
optionA: Yes; a correct upgrade removes the limit entirely
optionB: Yes; the new limit shows the wrong component was chosen
optionC: No; relieving one limit always exposes the next one, and the task did get faster
optionD: No, but the second limit means the first was not a limit at all
correctAnswerText: No; relieving one limit always exposes the next one, and the task did get faster
explanation: Something is always the slowest part, so removing one bottleneck necessarily reveals another. Whether the upgrade was worth it is settled by how much faster the task became, not by whether a limit remains.

prompt: Two upgrades are affordable and only one can be bought. One removes a limit that costs the task ten minutes a day; the other removes a limit costing two minutes a day and is cheaper. How should the choice be made?
optionA: Always the larger saving, since time matters most
optionB: By comparing what each buys against what each costs, since the larger saving is not automatically the better purchase
optionC: Always the cheaper one, since budgets are limited
optionD: Neither; both limits should be removed together
correctAnswerText: By comparing what each buys against what each costs, since the larger saving is not automatically the better purchase
explanation: Two quantities are in play and neither dominates by itself, so the decision needs both. A rule that looks only at the saving, or only at the price, is a preference standing in for a calculation.

prompt: A machine is needed to hold a very large archive that is read rarely, and the budget is tight. Speed is explicitly not a priority. Which configuration is defensible?
optionA: The fastest drive available, at whatever capacity fits the budget
optionB: A large amount of working memory instead of storage
optionC: A configuration that is fastest, largest and cheapest at once
optionD: A large, slower drive, accepting that reads take longer
correctAnswerText: A large, slower drive, accepting that reads take longer
explanation: The stated priorities are capacity and cost, and the answer gives up the thing that was said not to matter. The last option claims to win on every axis, which is what the trade-off says is unavailable.

prompt: A machine must serve a small dataset to many users as quickly as possible, and capacity is not a concern. The whole dataset fits comfortably in memory. Which configuration is defensible?
optionA: Enough memory to hold the dataset, and a fast processor, with modest storage
optionB: The largest storage drive available
optionC: Minimal memory, with the dataset read from storage each time
optionD: A configuration chosen for lowest cost across every component
correctAnswerText: Enough memory to hold the dataset, and a fast processor, with modest storage
explanation: The stated priority is speed for a small dataset, and the stem confirms it fits in memory, which removes the reason to buy capacity. Reading from storage each time gives up exactly what was asked for.

prompt: A supplier claims a configuration that is faster, larger and cheaper than every alternative. What is the first thing to check?
optionA: Nothing; a better configuration is simply better
optionB: Whether the price includes delivery
optionC: What it gives up that the comparison did not measure — durability, reliability, or how the figures were obtained
optionD: Whether the components are from the same manufacturer
correctAnswerText: What it gives up that the comparison did not measure — durability, reliability, or how the figures were obtained
explanation: Winning on every axis at once is what the trade-off says does not happen, so the claim points at an axis nobody compared. That is a reason to look harder rather than to reject it outright.

prompt: A budget can buy either much more memory or a much faster processor. The workload is not yet known. What follows?
optionA: Buy the processor, since it affects everything
optionB: The choice cannot be made responsibly yet; what the workload spends its time on is what decides it
optionC: Buy the memory, since it is more flexible
optionD: Split the budget evenly between the two
correctAnswerText: The choice cannot be made responsibly yet; what the workload spends its time on is what decides it
explanation: Which component matters is a property of the work rather than of the machine, so an unknown workload leaves the question genuinely open. Splitting evenly is a way of avoiding the decision rather than making it.

prompt: A configuration is chosen for a workload and the workload later changes character entirely. What does that say about the original decision?
optionA: It was wrong, since the configuration no longer suits the work
optionB: It was right, and the workload should be changed back
optionC: It says nothing, since hardware decisions cannot be judged
optionD: It may have been right when it was made; a decision is judged on what was known then, and the configuration should now be revisited
correctAnswerText: It may have been right when it was made; a decision is judged on what was known then, and the configuration should now be revisited
explanation: A choice made well on the information available can be overtaken by events, and treating that as an error discourages making any decision at all. What follows is a fresh decision rather than a verdict on the old one.

prompt: A workload reads one small table over and over while streaming a very large file past it once. The table is far smaller than memory and the file is far larger. Which layer does the work depend on most?
optionA: Memory, to hold the small table, while the large file is read from storage as it goes
optionB: Storage, since the file dominates the data volume
optionC: Registers, since the table is small
optionD: Cache alone, since the table is read repeatedly
correctAnswerText: Memory, to hold the small table, while the large file is read from storage as it goes
explanation: The two parts of the workload have different needs and each lands on a different layer. The table is what is read repeatedly and must therefore be held close; the file is read once and has nowhere else to be.

prompt: A workload holds a dataset slightly larger than the machine's memory and touches all of it constantly. The processor is idle much of the time. Which layer decides how fast it runs?
optionA: The processor, since it does the work
optionB: Registers, since every value passes through them
optionC: Storage, because the part that will not fit is fetched from there again and again
optionD: Memory, since the dataset is nearly small enough to fit
correctAnswerText: Storage, because the part that will not fit is fetched from there again and again
explanation: Being slightly too large is the worst case: almost everything fits, and the small remainder is fetched from the slowest layer constantly. An idle processor confirms the wait is elsewhere.

prompt: A dataset just fits in memory, and it then grows by a few per cent. Performance falls off a cliff rather than degrading gently. Why?
optionA: Memory becomes slower as it fills
optionB: The part that no longer fits is fetched from storage repeatedly, and storage is far slower rather than slightly slower
optionC: The processor throttles itself when memory is full
optionD: The growth was larger than reported
correctAnswerText: The part that no longer fits is fetched from storage repeatedly, and storage is far slower rather than slightly slower
explanation: The layers differ by large factors rather than small ones, so crossing from one to the next is a step rather than a slope. A few per cent more data can move a large share of the accesses to a layer orders of magnitude slower.

prompt: A colleague suggests that keeping data in the fastest available layer is always the right choice. When does that advice fail?
optionA: Never; faster is always better
optionB: Whenever the data is read only once, since speed is wasted
optionC: Whenever the data must survive a restart, since fast layers are less reliable
optionD: Whenever the data does not fit; a layer that is faster and too small does not hold the data at all
correctAnswerText: Whenever the data does not fit; a layer that is faster and too small does not hold the data at all
explanation: Capacity is a constraint rather than a preference, so the fastest layer is only a candidate if the data fits in it. Reading data once is a weaker objection — speed still helps, it simply helps less.
